14:5.ar: وَلَقَدۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مُوسَىٰ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَآ أَنۡ أَخۡرِجۡ قَوۡمَكَ مِنَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ إِلَى ٱلنُّورِ وَذَكِّرۡهُم بِأَيَّىٰمِ ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّكُلِّ صَبَّارࣲ شَكُورࣲ‏
14:5.en: We verily sent Moses with Our revelations, saying: Bring thy people forth from darkness unto light. And remind them of the days of Allah. Lo! therein are revelations for each steadfast, thankful (heart)

14:6.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِ ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَةَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِذۡ أَنجَىٰكُم مِّنۡ ءَالِ فِرۡعَوۡنَ يَسُومُونَكُمۡ سُوٓءَ ٱلۡعَذَابِ وَيُذَبِّحُونَ أَبۡنَآءَكُمۡ وَيَسۡتَحۡيُونَ نِسَآءَكُمۡۚ وَفِي ذَٰلِكُم بَلَآءࣱ مِّن رَّبِّكُمۡ عَظِيمࣱ‏
14:6.en: And (remind them) how Moses said unto his people: Remember Allah's favour unto you when He delivered you from Pharaoh's folk who were afflicting you with dreadful torment, and were slaying your sons and sparing your women; that was a tremendous trial from your Lord

14:35.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِيمُ رَبِّ ٱجۡعَلۡ هَٰذَا ٱلۡبَلَدَ ءَامِنࣰ ا وَٱجۡنُبۡنِي وَبَنِيَّ أَن نَّعۡبُدَ ٱلۡأَصۡنَامَ
14:35.en: And when Abraham said: My Lord! Make safe this territory, and preserve me and my sons from serving idols

14:36.ar: رَبِّ إِنَّهُنَّ أَضۡلَلۡنَ كَثِيرࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِۖ فَمَن تَبِعَنِي فَإِنَّهُۥ مِنِّيۖ وَمَنۡ عَصَانِي فَإِنَّكَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
14:36.en: My Lord! Lo! they have led many of mankind astray. But whoso followeth me, he verily is of me. And whoso disobeyeth me - Still Thou art Forgiving, Merciful

14:37.ar: رَّبَّنَآ إِنِّيٓ أَسۡكَنتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِي بِوَادٍ غَيۡرِ ذِي زَرۡعٍ عِندَ بَيۡتِكَ ٱلۡمُحَرَّمِ رَبَّنَا لِيُقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ فَٱجۡعَلۡ أَفۡـِٔدَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ تَهۡوِيٓ إِلَيۡهِمۡ وَٱرۡزُقۡهُم مِّنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَشۡكُرُونَ
14:37.en: Our Lord! Lo! I have settled some of my posterity in an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House, our Lord! that they may establish proper worship; so incline some hearts of men that they may yearn toward them, and provide Thou them with fruits in order that they may be thankful

14:38.ar: رَبَّنَآ إِنَّكَ تَعۡلَمُ مَا نُخۡفِي وَمَا نُعۡلِنُۗ وَمَا يَخۡفَىٰ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مِن شَيۡءࣲ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَلَا فِي ٱلسَّمَآءِ
14:38.en: Our Lord! Lo! Thou knowest that which we hide and that which we proclaim. Nothing in the earth or in the heaven is hidden from Allah

14:39.ar: ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِي وَهَبَ لِي عَلَى ٱلۡكِبَرِ إِسۡمَٰعِيلَ وَإِسۡحَٰقَۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي لَسَمِيعُ ٱلدُّعَآءِ
14:39.en: Praise be to Allah Who hath given me, in my old age, Ishmael and Isaac! Lo! my Lord is indeed the Hearer of Prayer

15:87.ar: وَلَقَدۡ ءَاتَيۡنَٰكَ سَبۡعࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلۡمَثَانِي وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ ٱلۡعَظِيمَ
15:87.en: We have given thee seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the great Qur'an

15:88.ar: لَا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيۡنَيۡكَ إِلَىٰ مَا مَتَّعۡنَا بِهِۦٓ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ وَلَا تَحۡزَنۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَٱخۡفِضۡ جَنَاحَكَ لِلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
15:88.en: Strain not thine eyes toward that which We cause some wedded pairs among them to enjoin, and be not grieved on their account, and lower thy wing (in tenderness) for the believers

16:53.ar: وَمَا بِكُم مِّن نِّعۡمَةࣲ فَمِنَ ٱللَّهِۖ ثُمَّ إِذَا مَسَّكُمُ ٱلضُّرُّ فَإِلَيۡهِ تَجۡـَٔرُونَ
16:53.en: And whatever of comfort ye enjoy, it is from Allah. Then, when misfortune reacheth you, unto Him ye cry for help

16:54.ar: ثُمَّ إِذَا كَشَفَ ٱلضُّرَّ عَنكُمۡ إِذَا فَرِيقࣱ مِّنكُم بِرَبِّهِمۡ يُشۡرِكُونَ
16:54.en: And afterward, when He hath rid you of the misfortune, behold! a set of you attribute partners to their Lord

93:11.en: Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse

20:131.ar: وَلَا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيۡنَيۡكَ إِلَىٰ مَا مَتَّعۡنَا بِهِۦٓ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ زَهۡرَةَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا لِنَفۡتِنَهُمۡ فِيهِۚ وَرِزۡقُ رَبِّكَ خَيۡرࣱ وَأَبۡقَىٰ
20:131.en: And strain not thine eyes toward that which We cause some wedded pairs among them to enjoy, the flower of the life of the world, that We may try them thereby. The provision of thy Lord is better and more lasting

34:13.ar: يَعۡمَلُونَ لَهُۥ مَا يَشَآءُ مِن مَّحَٰرِيبَ وَتَمَٰثِيلَ وَجِفَانࣲ كَٱلۡجَوَابِ وَقُدُورࣲ رَّاسِيَٰتٍۚ ٱعۡمَلُوٓاْ ءَالَ دَاوُۥدَ شُكۡرࣰ اۚ وَقَلِيلࣱ مِّنۡ عِبَادِيَ ٱلشَّكُورُ
34:13.en: They made for him what he willed: synagogues and statues, basins like wells and boilers built into the ground. Give thanks, O House of David! Few of My bondmen are thankful

9c71K1Y9jo4.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 13: Quranic Themes, Appreciating Blessings
9c71K1Y9jo4.one_line: Recognizing and using Allah's blessings: hardship as untaxed reward, the days of Allah, Ibrahim's gratitude, the Quran as the greatest gift, and crediting every good to Allah.
9c71K1Y9jo4.summary: He argues that the Quran trains believers to recognize blessings, including hardships whose value appears only later: there is no growth without friction, and a difficulty met with patience is pure reward, while ease carries heavy accountability, which is why Umar hoped only to break even. Musa was told to remind his people of the days of Allah, and he relates this to the sudden fall of the regime in Syria, which he still struggles to absorb; it helped him understand why Bani Isra'il faltered after so swift a deliverance, and leaves his generation no excuse but gratitude. In Ibrahim's dua at the Kaaba he notes that security came first, that Ibrahim hoped even for those who disobeyed him, and that provision was asked so people would be grateful. Gratitude is shown by using a blessing for others, and children should be coached to see their opportunities. From Al-Hijr he says the seven oft-repeated verses and the Quran outweigh anything others possess, so do not stare over the fence, and let the gift humble you. From An-Nahl he teaches that every blessing comes from Allah alone, that one should thank His means, and that turning to Him only in hardship is hypocrisy.

outline.heading: Blessings, a leading Quranic theme
outline.gist: The Quran asks us to recognize blessings from many angles, to know their source, and to see that even hardship can be one.

outline.heading: Hardship is a blessing you have not yet recognized
outline.gist: There is no growth without friction, and the hardest thing you persevered through often turns out to be your greatest blessing.

outline.heading: Ease is taxed, hardship is not
outline.gist: Wealth, health and long life bring questions on the Day of Judgment, while patience in loss or illness earns reward with nothing owed, so the best many can hope for with ease is to break even.

outline.heading: Umar's hope to break even
outline.gist: Umar told Abu Musa he was sure of his deeds with the Prophet but only hoped to break even on everything after; Abu Musa's son conceded Umar was wiser.

outline.heading: An ummah of praise
outline.gist: There is always reason to be grateful, seen and unseen, now and later.

outline.heading: Remind them of the days of Allah
outline.gist: Musa was sent to bring his people from darkness to light and to remind them how Allah saved them from Pharaoh's slaughter and enslavement.

outline.heading: How swiftly Allah changes reality
outline.gist: The fall of the regime in Syria within days, after thirteen years of war, seemed impossible to analysts, and he has still not processed it.

outline.heading: Understanding the exodus anew
outline.gist: A people enslaved for generations was free between dawn and midday, which helps him understand why they struggled to absorb it during the forty years.

outline.heading: The same dream for thirteen years
outline.gist: He dreams only of being back home as an outlaw, either escaping or caught; Bani Isra'il failed to hold on to the meaning of their day of Allah.

outline.heading: No excuse but gratitude
outline.gist: His generation must spend its days praising Allah for the removal of the tyrant; he introduces the closing verses of Surat Ibrahim.

outline.heading: First request: a land of security
outline.gist: Ibrahim asked for safety before anything else, because faith, ethics and practice cannot function without peace.

outline.heading: Keep me and my children from idols
outline.gist: He asked that he and his descendants be kept from idol worship, which had misled many.

outline.heading: Hope even for those who disobey
outline.gist: Ibrahim said that whoever disobeys him, Allah is forgiving and merciful, hoping good even for disbelievers.

outline.heading: A barren valley by Your sacred house
outline.gist: He left his family where nothing grew, by a house already there before he built it, and asked for provision so they would be grateful.

outline.heading: Praise for sons in old age
outline.gist: Ibrahim praised Allah for granting him Isma'il and Ishaq late in life, voicing his hopes for his nation and humanity.

outline.heading: Gratitude is itself a blessing
outline.gist: The one who holds a priceless gift without recognizing it can neither enjoy it nor be rewarded for gratitude.

outline.heading: Teach children what they have
outline.gist: Help the next generation see opportunities most people never had, through coaching and mentoring rather than strictness and anger.

outline.heading: Ibrahim was grateful with little
outline.gist: His dua was answered, yet in life he had little wealth and few followers, and he was grateful anyway.

outline.heading: Gratitude means using the blessing
outline.gist: Saying alhamdulillah is a duty, but true gratitude is putting blessings to beneficial use, which is what proclaiming Allah's favour means.

outline.heading: Seven oft-repeated gems
outline.gist: Al-mathani can mean precious pearls: the seven verses of Al-Fatihah, recited endlessly without losing benefit, alongside the whole Quran.

outline.heading: Al-Fatihah as the key
outline.gist: No other part of the Quran is recited in prayer before it; it validates everything after.

outline.heading: Do not stretch your eyes toward what others enjoy
outline.gist: Do not lose sight of the most valuable gift you carry by looking at others' wealth, status and ease.

outline.heading: Shaytan's whisper that the grass is greener
outline.gist: He tells you your luck has always been bad and others find gold behind every door, until you stop valuing what you have.

outline.heading: Do not grieve for them
outline.gist: The Prophet grieved that people were content with worldly wealth and would not listen; he was told he cannot change them.

outline.heading: The ultimate blessing humbles you
outline.gist: Lower your wing to the believers; generosity beyond measure leaves you silent, humbled and unable even to say thank you.

outline.heading: He left no money
outline.gist: The Prophet left nothing in wealth and his shield was in pawn, because he knew what the real blessing was.

outline.heading: Allah chose you
outline.gist: You could easily have lost your way; that you are in the masjid on a weeknight shows He chose you, which should humble you for life.

outline.heading: Every blessing is from Allah
outline.gist: Whatever good reaches you has one source; seeing a partner in its source is a serious failing.

outline.heading: Thank the means He uses
outline.gist: Thanking parents, employers and generous people is thanking Allah through the means He chose.

outline.heading: Take no credit yourself
outline.gist: Especially for what you think you partly earned, credit it all to Allah; the verse does not say from Allah and from yourselves.

outline.heading: Crying out to Him in hardship
outline.gist: When harm touches people they turn to Him loudly and insistently.

outline.heading: Remember Him at your highest too
outline.gist: If you turn to Him at your lowest, credit Him when life goes well; yet once relieved, some return to associating partners with Him.

outline.heading: Small gratitude prepares for eternal bliss
outline.gist: Life's events are lessons in perceiving Allah's decree; whoever cannot thank Him for little will not do well with an eternity of bliss.

outline.heading: He magnified every blessing
outline.gist: The Prophet treated even the smallest blessing as great; what we take for granted will be our downfall.

outline.heading: Blessings are not free
outline.gist: We owe it to use them for others; few servants are truly grateful, so ask to be among the few.

outline.heading: Entitlement versus contentment
outline.gist: Taking blessings for granted breeds entitlement and discontent; ambition is fine, but you must be grateful for the hand you have now to enjoy life.

themes.label: Syria

quran.point: Proclaiming Allah's favour means using it to benefit others, not showing it off.
A parallel verse calls what others enjoy the flower of this worldly life.
Few of Allah's servants are truly grateful.

hadith.gist: Umar asked Abu Musa whether he would accept keeping their deeds with the Prophet and breaking even on all deeds after; Umar wished for that, and Abu Musa's son admitted Umar was the wiser.
The Prophet died leaving no wealth, with his shield held in pawn.
A companion's description says the Prophet magnified every blessing, however small.
Umar prayed to be among the few who are grateful.

maxims: Without friction there is no growth
There is no tax on a difficulty you persevered through
True gratitude is using the blessing
They should be looking over the fence at you
What we take for granted will be our demise

stories.who: Umar and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
stories.point: Even the greatest companions feared accountability for the ease that came after the Prophet's time.

stories.who: Bani Isra'il after the crossing
stories.point: A deliverance too swift to absorb can be lost if its meaning is not held on to.

stories.who: Ibrahim at the Kaaba
stories.point: He asked for security and provision so that people would be grateful, and was grateful himself despite having little.

stories.who: The Prophet's pawned shield
stories.point: The real blessing is guidance and the Quran, not wealth.

contemporary: The fall of the Assad regime in Syria at the end of 2024, after thirteen to fourteen years of revolution and civil war
takeaways: Look back at hardships you persevered through and see them as your purest blessings
Show gratitude by putting each blessing to beneficial use, not only by saying alhamdulillah
Coach your children to recognize the opportunities they have that most people never had
Stop comparing yourself with others; treat the Quran as your greatest blessing and let it humble you
Credit every good thing to Allah, thank the people He uses as means, and turn to Him in ease as you do in hardship

10:84.ar: وَقَالَ مُوسَىٰ يَٰقَوۡمِ إِن كُنتُمۡ ءَامَنتُم بِٱللَّهِ فَعَلَيۡهِ تَوَكَّلُوٓاْ إِن كُنتُم مُّسۡلِمِينَ
10:84.en: And Moses said: O my people! If ye have believed in Allah then put trust in Him, if ye have indeed surrendered (unto Him)

10:85.ar: فَقَالُواْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ تَوَكَّلۡنَا رَبَّنَا لَا تَجۡعَلۡنَا فِتۡنَةࣰ لِّلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
10:85.en: They said: In Allah we put trust. Our Lord! Oh, make us not a lure for the wrongdoing folk

10:86.en: And, of Thy mercy, save us from the folk that disbelieve

10:87.ar: وَأَوۡحَيۡنَآ إِلَىٰ مُوسَىٰ وَأَخِيهِ أَن تَبَوَّءَا لِقَوۡمِكُمَا بِمِصۡرَ بُيُوتࣰ ا وَٱجۡعَلُواْ بُيُوتَكُمۡ قِبۡلَةࣰ وَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَۗ وَبَشِّرِ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
10:87.en: And We inspired Moses and his brother, (saying): Appoint houses for your people in Egypt and make your houses oratories, and establish worship. And give good news to the believers

11:12.ar: فَلَعَلَّكَ تَارِكُۢ بَعۡضَ مَا يُوحَىٰٓ إِلَيۡكَ وَضَآئِقُۢ بِهِۦ صَدۡرُكَ أَن يَقُولُواْ لَوۡلَآ أُنزِلَ عَلَيۡهِ كَنزٌ أَوۡ جَآءَ مَعَهُۥ مَلَكٌۚ إِنَّمَآ أَنتَ نَذِيرࣱۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ وَكِيلٌ
11:12.en: A likely thing, that thou wouldst forsake aught of that which hath been revealed unto thee, and that thy breast should be straitened for it, because they say: Why hath not a treasure been sent down for him, or an angel come with him? Thou art but a warner, and Allah is in charge of all things

11:54.ar: إِن نَّقُولُ إِلَّا ٱعۡتَرَىٰكَ بَعۡضُ ءَالِهَتِنَا بِسُوٓءࣲۗ قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أُشۡهِدُ ٱللَّهَ وَٱشۡهَدُوٓاْ أَنِّي بَرِيٓءࣱ مِّمَّا تُشۡرِكُونَ
11:54.en: We say naught save that one of our gods hath possessed thee in an evil way. He said: I call Allah to witness, and do ye (too) bear witness, that I am innocent of (all) that ye ascribe as partners (to Allah)

11:55.ar: مِن دُونِهِۦۖ فَكِيدُونِي جَمِيعࣰ ا ثُمَّ لَا تُنظِرُونِ
11:55.en: Beside Him. So (try to) circumvent me, all of you, give me no respite

11:56.ar: إِنِّي تَوَكَّلۡتُ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ رَبِّي وَرَبِّكُمۚ مَّا مِن دَآبَّةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ ءَاخِذُۢ بِنَاصِيَتِهَآۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي عَلَىٰ صِرَٰطࣲ مُّسۡتَقِيمࣲ‏
11:56.en: Lo! I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Not an animal but He doth grasp it by the forelock! Lo! my Lord is on a straight path

11:57.ar: فَإِن تَوَلَّوۡاْ فَقَدۡ أَبۡلَغۡتُكُم مَّآ أُرۡسِلۡتُ بِهِۦٓ إِلَيۡكُمۡۚ وَيَسۡتَخۡلِفُ رَبِّي قَوۡمًا غَيۡرَكُمۡ وَلَا تَضُرُّونَهُۥ شَيۡـًٔاۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءٍ حَفِيظࣱ‏
11:57.en: And if ye turn away, still I have conveyed unto you that wherewith I was sent unto you, and my Lord will set in place of you a folk other than you. Ye cannot injure Him at all. Lo! my Lord is Guardian over all things

85:4.en: (Self-)destroyed were the owners of the ditch

85:7.ar: وَهُمۡ عَلَىٰ مَا يَفۡعَلُونَ بِٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ شُهُودࣱ‏
85:7.en: And were themselves the witnesses of what they did to the believers

85:8.ar: وَمَا نَقَمُواْ مِنۡهُمۡ إِلَّآ أَن يُؤۡمِنُواْ بِٱللَّهِ ٱلۡعَزِيزِ ٱلۡحَمِيدِ
85:8.en: They had naught against them save that they believed in Allah, the Mighty, the Owner of Praise

60:5.ar: رَبَّنَا لَا تَجۡعَلۡنَا فِتۡنَةࣰ لِّلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ وَٱغۡفِرۡ لَنَا رَبَّنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ

1P8UCvMkFHY.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 11: Quranic Themes, Tawakkul
1P8UCvMkFHY.one_line: Tawakkul as effort, inner reliance and contentment, shown through Musa's people facing Pharaoh, the Prophet under Makkan pressure, and Hud defying his people.
1P8UCvMkFHY.summary: He pairs tawakkul with the previous night's theme of courage, since each produces the other. Tawakkul has three parts: doing your absolute best with what you have, depending inwardly on Allah for the outcome, which is its religious core, and being content with whatever He decrees. He tests understanding with a question: if you are fully prepared for an exam, do you still need tawakkul? Yes, because countless things can intervene; going in unprepared and hoping is hope, not tawakkul. From 10:84-86 he shows Musa telling an oppressed, frightened people that faith and submission require reliance on Allah before the dangerous step of leaving Pharaoh; their dua not to be made a trial for the oppressors shows Muslims do not seek victimhood. They reached the sea ready to make it or die trying. From 11:12 he describes the Prophet, distressed by Makkan demands for treasure and angels, being told he is only a warner: the miracle would be the people Islam transforms, so worry only about what you can change. From 11:54-57 Hud disowns his people's shirk and dares them to do their worst because he relies on Allah. He urges parents to teach their children this tool.

outline.heading: Tawakkul, twin of courage
outline.gist: One of the most important tools a Muslim carries, a way of life for every part of living, which children should learn once they start worrying about the future.

outline.heading: First element: trying your absolute best
outline.gist: Not perfection, but exhausting your resources within your circumstances; without this, whatever else you call it, it is not tawakkul.

outline.heading: Second element: inner dependence on Allah
outline.gist: The part that gives tawakkul its name and its religious core: knowing Allah delivers the outcomes and is steward of your affairs, which brings peace even in a storm.

outline.heading: Third element: contentment with the result
outline.gist: Accepting whatever Allah chooses, then dusting yourself off to try again or change route.

outline.heading: Tawakkul breeds courage: the cave
outline.gist: The Prophet in the cave is the ultimate example; you should also identify your own attempts at tawakkul and which element failed.

outline.heading: Why rely on Allah if fully prepared?
outline.gist: Even if you know the material and the questions, endless things can stop you passing, so tawakkul is always needed.

outline.heading: Unprepared hope is not tawakkul
outline.gist: Hoping against odds you could have controlled is allowed, but do not call it tawakkul, do not be proud of it, and know it is blameworthy.

outline.heading: Teach your children this tool
outline.gist: Sit with your children, answer their questions, and get the answers yourself first.

outline.heading: Musa's words at their lowest moment
outline.gist: As persecution worsened despite the signs and hope was thinnest, Musa told his people to rely on Allah.

outline.heading: Tawakkul conditioned by iman and islam
outline.gist: The command sits between two conditions, belief and submission, the theology and the practice that tawakkul needs.

outline.heading: The terror of rising against a dictator
outline.gist: Rebellion risks bloodshed, multiplied persecution and the loss of what little security an enslaved people has.

outline.heading: A people new to faith
outline.gist: Bani Isra'il had lost their connection to Allah until Musa returned, so the next step he taught them was reliance.

outline.heading: Do not make us a trial for the oppressors
outline.gist: They asked not to become the means of the oppressors' punishment by being killed and dispossessed, a dua repeated in the Quran.

outline.heading: No victim mentality
outline.gist: Muslims do not seek oppression; Islam cannot reach its full form under it, which is why the Prophet left Makkah.

outline.heading: The fear behind the dua
outline.gist: Like the believers thrown into the fire, the persecuted become a trial for their persecutors; they knew Musa was asking for a frightening ride.

outline.heading: Save us by Your mercy
outline.gist: They asked to be rescued from Pharaoh's people, and Musa was told to make their houses places of prayer and unite.

outline.heading: The exodus as rebellion
outline.gist: Slaves leaving without permission after nine signs was defiance; at the Red Sea, with the army behind and mostly women and children, no one knew what came next.

outline.heading: Relying on Allah before the frightening step
outline.gist: Tawakkul is needed when the right course is scary, costly and unpopular, and you leave what comes next to Allah.

outline.heading: Make it or die trying
outline.gist: Not every story ends with a staff that splits the sea; accepting any outcome is tawakkul, and Allah gave the land to the oppressed.

outline.heading: Perhaps you would leave part of the revelation
outline.gist: Allah addresses even a passing thought of the Prophet, a heavy life where every less-than-optimal thought is answered by revelation.

outline.heading: Our thoughts are free, his were addressed
outline.gist: Ordinary people are not held to account for passing thoughts; the Prophet faced death threats, murdered companions and the flight to Abyssinia.

outline.heading: The thought of toning it down
outline.gist: For a moment he wondered whether to soften part of the message, and felt the tightness in the chest the verse describes.

outline.heading: Children with guns demanding treasure and angels
outline.gist: Leaders who refused mature argument demanded a treasure or an angel as proof, while killing people for their beliefs.

outline.heading: Pharaoh's same demand of Musa
outline.gist: Pharaoh asked why Musa came without gold bracelets or accompanying angels; it is the same story every time.

outline.heading: Irrelevant demands as distraction
outline.gist: When an argument is strong, opponents change the subject because the status quo benefits them.

outline.heading: Change as an admission of fault
outline.gist: Most people would rather die than admit they were wrong, and Allah lets them hold on to it.

outline.heading: You are only a warner
outline.gist: He was not sent to produce wealth or wonders; the miracle of Islam would come after people accepted it.

outline.heading: The Muslim is the miracle
outline.gist: A civilization uniting religion, science and ethics was the proof; a community that is just and hardworking gets wealth and feels the angels' presence.

outline.heading: Allah is the trustee: do your part
outline.gist: Worrying about what you cannot change, like other people's minds, only weakens your defences and motivation.

outline.heading: Leave what you cannot change in Allah's hands
outline.gist: When dirt was thrown in his face and his daughter cried, he told her Allah would give her father victory, even if after his life.

outline.heading: Why the surah is named after Hud
outline.gist: Not the longest or most dramatic story, but Hud articulated what reform means; his people claimed a god had struck his mind.

outline.heading: Disowning their shirk
outline.gist: He called Allah and them to witness that he was free of their wrongdoing; you cannot meet an oppressor halfway, even under explicit death threats.

outline.heading: Do your worst
outline.gist: Like Nuh, Musa and Muhammad, he told them to plot together and give him no respite, without begging for anything.

outline.heading: I rely on Allah, my Lord and yours
outline.gist: His defiance came from tawakkul; every creature is held by its forelock and will be brought to account.

outline.heading: My Lord is on a straight path
outline.gist: Judgment will be fair with no injustice, so he would not stand down.

outline.heading: He did not know he would be saved
outline.gist: Most prophets were killed; Hud spoke with strength because he trusted Allah, not because he was promised safety.

37:51.ar: قَالَ قَآئِلࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ إِنِّي كَانَ لِي قَرِينࣱ‏

37:52.en: Who used to say: Art thou in truth of those who put faith (in his words)

37:53.ar: أَءِذَا مِتۡنَا وَكُنَّا تُرَابࣰ ا وَعِظَٰمًا أَءِنَّا لَمَدِينُونَ
37:53.en: Can we, when we are dead and have become mere dust and bones - can we (then) verily be brought to book

37:55.en: Then looketh he and seeth him in the depth of hell

37:56.en: He saith: By Allah, thou verily didst all but cause my ruin

37:57.ar: وَلَوۡلَا نِعۡمَةُ رَبِّي لَكُنتُ مِنَ ٱلۡمُحۡضَرِينَ
37:57.en: And had it not been for the favour of my Lord, I too had been of those haled forth (to doom)

37:58.en: Are we then not to die

37:59.ar: إِلَّا مَوۡتَتَنَا ٱلۡأُولَىٰ وَمَا نَحۡنُ بِمُعَذَّبِينَ
37:59.en: Saving our former death, and are we not to be punished

37:60.en: Lo! this is the supreme triumph

37:61.en: For the like of this, then, let the workers work

37:62.ar: أَذَٰلِكَ خَيۡرࣱ نُّزُلًا أَمۡ شَجَرَةُ ٱلزَّقُّومِ
37:62.en: Is this better as a welcome, or the tree of Zaqqum

37:63.en: Lo! We have appointed it a torment for wrong-doers

37:64.ar: إِنَّهَا شَجَرَةࣱ تَخۡرُجُ فِيٓ أَصۡلِ ٱلۡجَحِيمِ
37:64.en: Lo! it is a tree that springeth in the heart of hell

37:65.en: Its crop is as it were the heads of devils

37:66.ar: فَإِنَّهُمۡ لَأٓكِلُونَ مِنۡهَا فَمَالِـُٔونَ مِنۡهَا ٱلۡبُطُونَ
37:66.en: And lo! they verily must eat thereof, and fill (their) bellies therewith

37:67.ar: ثُمَّ إِنَّ لَهُمۡ عَلَيۡهَا لَشَوۡبࣰ ا مِّنۡ حَمِيمࣲ‏
37:67.en: And afterward, lo! thereupon they have a drink of boiling water

37:68.en: And afterward, lo! their return is surely unto hell

37:69.en: They indeed found their fathers astray

37:70.en: But they make haste (to follow) in their footsteps

37:71.en: And verily most of the men of old went astray before them

37:72.en: And verily We sent among them warners

37:73.en: Then see the nature of the consequence for those warned

37:27.en: And some of them draw near unto others, mutually questioning

37:28.ar: قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّكُمۡ كُنتُمۡ تَأۡتُونَنَا عَنِ ٱلۡيَمِينِ
37:28.en: They say: Lo! ye used to come unto us, imposing, (swearing that ye spoke the truth)

37:29.en: They answer: Nay, but ye (yourselves) were not believers

37:30.ar: وَمَا كَانَ لَنَا عَلَيۡكُم مِّن سُلۡطَٰنِۭۖ بَلۡ كُنتُمۡ قَوۡمࣰ ا طَٰغِينَ
37:30.en: We had no power over you, but ye were wayward folk

37:31.ar: فَحَقَّ عَلَيۡنَا قَوۡلُ رَبِّنَآۖ إِنَّا لَذَآئِقُونَ
37:31.en: Now the Word of our Lord hath been fulfilled concerning us. Lo! we are about to taste (the doom)

37:32.en: Thus we misled you. Lo! we were (ourselves) astray

37:33.en: Then lo! this day they (both) are sharers in the doom

37:34.en: Lo! thus deal We with the guilty

37:35.ar: إِنَّهُمۡ كَانُوٓاْ إِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمۡ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ يَسۡتَكۡبِرُونَ
37:35.en: For when it was said unto them, There is no Allah save Allah, they were scornful

37:36.en: And said: Shall we forsake our gods for a mad poet

37:37.en: Nay, but he brought the Truth, and he confirmed those sent (before him)

37:39.ar: وَمَا تُجۡزَوۡنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
37:39.en: Ye are requited naught save what ye did

37:41.en: For them there is a known provision

37:42.en: Fruits. And they will be honoured

37:45.en: A cup from a gushing spring is brought round for them

37:47.ar: لَا فِيهَا غَوۡلࣱ وَلَا هُمۡ عَنۡهَا يُنزَفُونَ
37:47.en: Wherein there is no headache nor are they made mad thereby

37:48.en: And with them are those of modest gaze, with lovely eyes

37:49.en: (Pure) as they were hidden eggs (of the ostrich)

37:50.en: And some of them draw near unto others, mutually questioning

35:9.ar: وَٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِيٓ أَرۡسَلَ ٱلرِّيَٰحَ فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابࣰ ا فَسُقۡنَٰهُ إِلَىٰ بَلَدࣲ مَّيِّتࣲ فَأَحۡيَيۡنَا بِهِ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ بَعۡدَ مَوۡتِهَاۚ كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ

70:4.ar: تَعۡرُجُ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ وَٱلرُّوحُ إِلَيۡهِ فِي يَوۡمࣲ كَانَ مِقۡدَارُهُۥ خَمۡسِينَ أَلۡفَ سَنَةࣲ‏
70:4.en: (Whereby) the angels and the Spirit ascend unto Him in a Day whereof the span is fifty thousand years

2:170.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُواْ بَلۡ نَتَّبِعُ مَآ أَلۡفَيۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَنَآۚ أَوَلَوۡ كَانَ ءَابَآؤُهُمۡ لَا يَعۡقِلُونَ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا يَهۡتَدُونَ
2:170.en: And when it is said unto them: Follow that which Allah hath revealed, they say: We follow that wherein we found our fathers. What! Even though their fathers were wholly unintelligent and had no guidance

6wursz7Qhq8.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Saffat, Part 4: Verses 51-74
6wursz7Qhq8.one_line: A man in Paradise recalls the friend who mocked resurrection, the tree of Zaqqum, and the danger of blindly following one's forefathers.
6wursz7Qhq8.summary: He opens by noting that people on Judgment Day ask each other the questions they should have asked in life, when the answers could still change their destination. In verses 51-53 a believer in Paradise remembers a close companion who kept asking, with a mocking triple question, whether he really believed in being raised from dust and bone. The sheikh calls this the central weakness of the ummah today: many only half believe in resurrection, but certainty admits only yes or no. If doubt lingers, at least live as if you believe, so that your book shows no trace of it; he points to dead land revived by rain as constant evidence. The believer answered yes and the friendship cooled, since closeness needs a shared framework. Looking down, he sees his friend in the middle of Hell and credits only his Lord's blessing, not his own grit, for being spared. Judgment Day teaches whatever lessons one failed to learn in life, which is why it can last fifty thousand years for some and a prayer's length for others. The people of Paradise rejoice that they will never die again: this is the true win. Zaqqum and boiling drink await those who rushed after their misguided forefathers, so a Muslim questions inherited habits and culture. Only the servants Allah has made sincere escape, and sincerity is the ultimate gift to ask for.

outline.heading: Turning to one another on Judgment Day
outline.gist: The long passage of the unseen continues; people questioning one another after the reckoning is a revealing image.

outline.heading: Ask the questions now, while they matter
outline.gist: The same questions will be asked and answered on that day, but only answers found in this life change your destination.

outline.heading: Recap: leaders, followers and the sincere servants
outline.gist: The misled and misleaders share the punishment, except Allah's chosen sincere servants who enjoy every pleasure of Paradise.

outline.heading: The people of Paradise also ask each other
outline.gist: Their questions are ones they had already asked and answered in life.

outline.heading: 'I had a qarin': the meaning of companion
outline.gist: Qarin is something always paired with you, hence a close friend; a man reclining in Paradise remembers one.

outline.heading: The friend's mocking question about resurrection
outline.gist: Do you really believe that after we become dust and bones we will be raised and held to account?

outline.heading: Three question particles for one question
outline.gist: Repeating the question marker is not normal Arabic; it signals mockery and the absurdity he sees in the belief.

outline.heading: The question that weakens the ummah
outline.gist: 'You don't really believe this, do you?' is the central problem of Muslims today; put the question to yourself.

outline.heading: Certainty is only yes or no
outline.gist: Anything short of certain yes is a no; this question cannot carry a complex answer.

outline.heading: If you doubt, at least live as if you believe
outline.gist: Many 'kind of' believe; quoting a philosopher, he urges that our choices show no doubt even if some lingers inside.

outline.heading: Behaviour reveals belief in resurrection
outline.gist: How we treat people, speak, earn and prioritise shows how much we fear being questioned.

outline.heading: Dead land revived: evidence seen a million times
outline.gist: Rain revives dead earth again and again; nature dies and returns, so why would we be any different?

azZSv29U5pw.title: Quranic Themes: Ethical Consistency
azZSv29U5pw.one_line: An ethic is only an ethic when held consistently, even when inconvenient, shown through Yusuf's chastity, his forgiveness of his brothers, and covenant-keeping.
azZSv29U5pw.summary: He presents ethical consistency as one of the Quran's top ten themes. A value practised only when convenient is a preference, and the Quran rewards ethics, not preferences. Every ethic has exceptions built into its definition, such as concealing the truth from an enemy in war or smoothing a reconciliation, so values need robust definitions, but once defined they must hold always: the generous give even when poor, if only time or a listening ear. An ethic is proven only when it becomes inconvenient. The Prophet was the same man at 42 with nothing and at 60 ruling most of Arabia; opinions should grow, ethics should not. Through Surah Yusuf he shows a young man with every condition for sin, alone, enslaved, unknown and pursued, who refused and preferred prison, because chastity was an ethic laid down by age six. Along the way he warns that attention is our most valuable possession and that delaying marriage into the thirties is heading toward a social catastrophe the community must face. Yusuf's second test was forgiving brothers who stole forty years of his life; he engineered their admission so he could forgive at once, words the Prophet later used himself. He ends with 13:19-20: keep your covenant and your word.

outline.heading: Ethical consistency: one of the Quran's top themes
outline.gist: An ethic that is not consistent cannot be called an ethic; it is a preference.

outline.heading: Ethics, values and principles are defined by consistency
outline.gist: The terms are close to interchangeable, and any condition placed on them removes the name.

outline.heading: Exceptions are part of the definition
outline.gist: Not telling an enemy the truth in war, a kind compliment, or easing a reconciliation do not break honesty because they are built into it.

outline.heading: Values are not meant to make you naive
outline.gist: Honesty does not mean confessing your sins publicly; values need robust definitions to be practised wisely.

outline.heading: Generosity when poor: ethics versus preferences
outline.gist: The generous give a lot when rich and a little when poor, even time or an ear; the Quran offers Paradise to ethics, not preferences.

outline.heading: It's only an ethic when it's inconvenient
outline.gist: Muslims rarely grasp this theme; failing to practise a value when it costs you means it was never yours.

outline.heading: From a nice idea to a lived value
outline.gist: Moving from admiring a story to practising it is a gap that takes deliberate work.

outline.heading: The Prophet was the same man in weakness and in rule
outline.gist: Whether met at 42 with nothing or at 60 ruling most of Arabia, his ethics and treatment of people never changed.

outline.heading: Opinions should grow; ethics should not
outline.gist: Never changing your mind in ten years means you learned nothing, but honesty is not an opinion and should stay constant.

outline.heading: Surah Yusuf: lessons a child can draw out
outline.gist: Some surahs still hide their code, but Yusuf's lessons are plain enough for anyone who reflects.

outline.heading: Yusuf's brothers envied their father's attention
outline.gist: An idyllic childhood ended when envy over their father's attention grew enough for them to try to kill him.

outline.heading: Attention is your most valuable possession
outline.gist: Free apps are the most expensive because they harvest attention; a three-year-old wants only to be watched.

outline.heading: Seek Allah's attention; give yours only to the worthy
outline.gist: What we really crave is Allah looking at us with mercy; money comes and goes, but attention should not be given out for free.

outline.heading: The noble son of the noble, enslaved in Egypt
outline.gist: A fourth-generation prophet whose lineage meant nothing in a foreign land, a capable seventeen-year-old shaped by hardship.

outline.heading: Every condition for temptation was present
outline.gist: Young, unknown, enslaved and held to no standard, pursued in his own house by an attractive woman: a scenario people would pay for.

outline.heading: Murawadah: being asked to give up your integrity
outline.gist: She asked him to give up something personal, his purity, which to him was an ethic.

outline.heading: Chastity as an ethic Muslim youth no longer know
outline.gist: His surveys find under a third of Muslim youth understand 'iffah; sexuality is sacred, not for sale or casual indulgence.

outline.heading: Why Yusuf was not embittered
outline.gist: Betrayed and stripped of everything at six, he could have turned to crime; instead his ethical foundation held at seventeen.

outline.heading: I seek refuge in Allah; the proof of his Lord
outline.gist: He refused to betray the one who housed him; the proof of his Lord was his existing clarity, not a sudden miracle, despite strange tafsir claims.

outline.heading: He never even moved toward it
outline.gist: Read correctly, the conditional means he made no move and had no intention; Allah turned evil away from His sincere servant.

outline.heading: Her confession and his choice of prison
outline.gist: She admitted he held fast and left no opening; when the city's women joined in, he asked for prison over sin.

outline.heading: Prison over a night of sin: a different mentality
outline.gist: Some would serve a year in jail for a night with someone; young men today must be very careful.

outline.heading: Delayed marriage is heading toward catastrophe
outline.gist: He married by 25 while studying medicine and sharia; people unmarried into their thirties point to a problem we ignore.

outline.heading: Distorted sexuality harms families; speak openly
outline.gist: Too much, no or wrong access to intimacy distorts sexuality and harms people; Muslims in the West must address it directly.

outline.heading: A story we could not believe had Allah not told it
outline.gist: Reading it should make us ask whether our own ethics are as consistent as we think.

outline.heading: What his brothers took from him
outline.gist: The well, slavery, nine years in prison, slander, and forty years without seeing his parents.

outline.heading: He maneuvered so they would admit and he could forgive
outline.gist: Instead of a revenge saga he hid his identity so they would feel shame, confess, and let him forgive and keep the family whole.

outline.heading: Forty years without remorse
outline.gist: They never came clean to their father, showing almost no remorse, which makes his forgiveness harder to fathom.

outline.heading: Their admission: Allah has preferred you over us
outline.gist: Humbled, the brothers admitted Allah had favoured him and that they had been at fault.

outline.heading: No blame on you today; Abu Sufyan seeks a way back
outline.gist: Without missing a beat Yusuf forgave; later Ali coached Abu Sufyan to approach the Prophet with the brothers' words.

outline.heading: The Prophet answers with Yusuf's words
outline.gist: Though angry at his betrayal, the Prophet replied immediately with Yusuf's reply, having waited for the chance to live it.

outline.heading: Learn a verse, then wait for the chance to practise it
outline.gist: Knowing the Quran means listening for its lesson and practising it the moment life offers the opportunity.

outline.heading: Those who keep Allah's covenant and their word
outline.gist: People of intellect fulfil their covenants whether convenient or not; we gave our word to live by the book and must keep it.

dwydq6XipGg.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 8: Humbleness, Part 2 (Arrogance)
dwydq6XipGg.one_line: Arrogance as self-worth built on comparison with others, illustrated through Iblis, and cured by focusing on one's own sins and serving people.
dwydq6XipGg.summary: Continuing his series on humbleness as the balance between confidence and humility, he moves from vanity to arrogance. Vanity is over-crediting yourself for what you achieve; arrogance is ranking yourself against people you see as peers. He shows how quickly people size others up, reduce them to a word, and hunt for one flaw in anyone who threatens the thing they draw value from. Most of tazkiyah, he argues, is separating what you know from what you assume, and you only truly know your own sins, so you have no basis to rank yourself above anyone, least of all through religiosity, since nobody knows how anyone's life will end. Iblis is the Quran's case study: great worship and closeness did not protect him once he let comparison fester, and even claiming certainty that you would have bowed is the same trap. The cure is preoccupation with your own faults and seeking forgiveness. Humbleness shows itself in service: a servant of Allah cannot carry an ego, so believers should compete in serving others. Value to a team is not self-value; when self-worth rests on Allah, insults and flattery no longer move you, though you still correct bad behaviour. He closes with a warning that knowledge without humbleness harms, and a story about the hidden arrogance of a renowned imam.

outline.heading: Humbleness and its four opposites
outline.gist: Humbleness combines confidence and humility; its opposites are vanity and arrogance on one side and low self-esteem on the other.

outline.heading: Knowing your skills is not vanity; praising others is a duty
outline.gist: Saying you are good at something is fine unless it raises your self-value. We must recognise others' qualities, though the Prophet warned against flattery that breaks a person's back.

outline.heading: Pulling the pendulum back to the middle
outline.gist: Against vanity, remember how your goals were really achieved; against low self-worth, remember Allah placed divine potential in you. Much of tazkiyah is mental exercise.

outline.heading: Arrogance defined: ranking yourself against peers
outline.gist: Arrogance needs other people; it is how you see yourself compared to someone you accept as a peer.

outline.heading: Sizing people up and reducing them to a word
outline.gist: We judge newcomers instantly and fill gaps with assumptions; calling someone arrogant is a grave judgment that demeans the complexity of a human being.

outline.heading: Hunting for flaws in someone who threatens you
outline.gist: When someone is better in the field you draw value from, you search their life until you find one thing you do better.

outline.heading: Compete with your past self, not others
outline.gist: If you feel good because others are less, you will feel less when others are good. Nobody starts from the same point.

outline.heading: Knowing versus assuming
outline.gist: Ninety percent of tazkiyah is separating knowledge from assumption; you may not judge on assumption, and Allah asks for good assumptions of people outside business and marriage decisions.

outline.heading: The mentor's exception: assuming problems in order to teach
outline.gist: With students and children he deliberately assumes problems so he can catch and correct them.

outline.heading: Never feel superior through religiosity
outline.gist: Using guidance to look down on others is among the worst things, since nobody knows who is closer to Allah or how anyone will end.

outline.heading: Iblis: closeness to Allah undone by comparison
outline.gist: Iblis worshipped until he was raised among the angels, yet let arrogance fester and refused to honour Adam on the grounds of merit and origin.

outline.heading: Claiming you would have bowed is the same trap
outline.gist: Being certain you would have obeyed in his place is itself arrogance; you can only hope and ask Allah to make you one who prostrates.

outline.heading: Could you serve the person you despise most?
outline.gist: A thought exercise to feel Iblis's test; he was offered a way out and still chose Hell to prove his point.

outline.heading: The antidote: preoccupation with your own sins
outline.gist: If you are busy with your own faults and seeking forgiveness, you have no time to search for others' flaws; you know your sins but only assume theirs.

outline.heading: Humbleness is seeing reality, even with siblings
outline.gist: Humbleness is not inferiority but recognising you know nothing of others' inner lives, even a twin's; your value is fixed and needs no proof.

outline.heading: Value to a team is not self-value
outline.gist: He is valuable on an oncology team and useless on a basketball team; you must prove usefulness to your team, but it must not touch your worth before Allah.

outline.heading: Humbleness shows itself in service
outline.gist: A servant with an ego is useless to his master; being Allah's servant contradicts carrying an ego.

outline.heading: Competing in service instead of status
outline.gist: Stop comparing popularity, wealth or wit; Allah judges how good a servant you were, so compete to serve others more.

outline.heading: Secure self-value is untouched by insults, but no doormat
outline.gist: Anger at rudeness means you still draw value from status; the Prophet was unmoved by what people said. You still correct bad behaviour calmly.

outline.heading: Turning the table: assume good and serve
outline.gist: We do the opposite of what Allah wants: assuming the worst, feeling entitled to be served. Reverse it and you live better.

outline.heading: Teach youth they need not prove their worth
outline.gist: Compete with yourself over time; children must learn their value is already there.

outline.heading: When the pendulum gets stuck
outline.gist: Narcissism fixes it at one end and some mental illnesses at the other; both need support, therapy and sometimes medication.

outline.heading: Knowledge without humbleness leads to ruin
outline.gist: Without humbleness, everything learned feeds vanity and arrogance; even a speck of arrogance bars entry to Paradise.

outline.heading: The elderly sheikh's story of Iblis's hooks
outline.gist: An old scholar being venerated told of a famous imam who dreamt Iblis prepared hooks for everyone but him, and was offended until told he needed none.

7:33.ar: قُلۡ إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ رَبِّيَ ٱلۡفَوَٰحِشَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنۡهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ وَٱلۡإِثۡمَ وَٱلۡبَغۡيَ بِغَيۡرِ ٱلۡحَقِّ وَأَن تُشۡرِكُواْ بِٱللَّهِ مَا لَمۡ يُنَزِّلۡ بِهِۦ سُلۡطَٰنࣰ ا وَأَن تَقُولُواْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
7:33.en: Say: My Lord forbiddeth only indecencies, such of them as are apparent and such as are within, and sin and wrongful oppression, and that ye associate with Allah that for which no warrant hath been revealed, and that ye tell concerning Allah that which ye know not

7:80.ar: وَلُوطًا إِذۡ قَالَ لِقَوۡمِهِۦٓ أَتَأۡتُونَ ٱلۡفَٰحِشَةَ مَا سَبَقَكُم بِهَا مِنۡ أَحَدࣲ مِّنَ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
7:80.en: And Lot! (Remember) when he said unto his folk: Will ye commit abomination such as no creature ever did before you

7:81.ar: إِنَّكُمۡ لَتَأۡتُونَ ٱلرِّجَالَ شَهۡوَةࣰ مِّن دُونِ ٱلنِّسَآءِۚ بَلۡ أَنتُمۡ قَوۡمࣱ مُّسۡرِفُونَ
7:81.en: Lo! ye come with lust unto men instead of women. Nay, but ye are wanton folk

7:82.ar: وَمَا كَانَ جَوَابَ قَوۡمِهِۦٓ إِلَّآ أَن قَالُوٓاْ أَخۡرِجُوهُم مِّن قَرۡيَتِكُمۡۖ إِنَّهُمۡ أُنَاسࣱ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ
7:82.en: And the answer of his people was only that they said (one to another): Turn them out of your township. They are folk, forsooth, who keep pure

7:83.ar: فَأَنجَيۡنَٰهُ وَأَهۡلَهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱمۡرَأَتَهُۥ كَانَتۡ مِنَ ٱلۡغَٰبِرِينَ
7:83.en: And We rescued him and his household, save his wife, who was of those who stayed behind

7:84.ar: وَأَمۡطَرۡنَا عَلَيۡهِم مَّطَرࣰ اۖ فَٱنظُرۡ كَيۡفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلۡمُجۡرِمِينَ
7:84.en: And We rained a rain upon them. See now the nature of the consequence of evil-doers

7:156.ar: ۞وَٱكۡتُبۡ لَنَا فِي هَٰذِهِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا حَسَنَةࣰ وَفِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ إِنَّا هُدۡنَآ إِلَيۡكَۚ قَالَ عَذَابِيٓ أُصِيبُ بِهِۦ مَنۡ أَشَآءُۖ وَرَحۡمَتِي وَسِعَتۡ كُلَّ شَيۡءࣲۚ فَسَأَكۡتُبُهَا لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ وَيُؤۡتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَٱلَّذِينَ هُم بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ
7:156.en: And ordain for us in this world that which is good, and in the Hereafter (that which is good), Lo! We have turned unto Thee. He said: I smite with My punishment whom I will, and My mercy embraceth all things, therefore I shall ordain it for those who ward off (evil) and pay the poor-due, and those who believe Our revelations

7:157.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ ٱلرَّسُولَ ٱلنَّبِيَّ ٱلۡأُمِّيَّ ٱلَّذِي يَجِدُونَهُۥ مَكۡتُوبًا عِندَهُمۡ فِي ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةِ وَٱلۡإِنجِيلِ يَأۡمُرُهُم بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَيَنۡهَىٰهُمۡ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَيُحِلُّ لَهُمُ ٱلطَّيِّبَٰتِ وَيُحَرِّمُ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡخَبَٰٓئِثَ وَيَضَعُ عَنۡهُمۡ إِصۡرَهُمۡ وَٱلۡأَغۡلَٰلَ ٱلَّتِي كَانَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡۚ فَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ بِهِۦ وَعَزَّرُوهُ وَنَصَرُوهُ وَٱتَّبَعُواْ ٱلنُّورَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أُنزِلَ مَعَهُۥٓ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ
7:157.en: Those who follow the messenger, the Prophet who can neither read nor write, whom they will find described in the Torah and the Gospel (which are) with them. He will enjoin on them that which is right and forbid them that which is wrong. He will make lawful for them all good things and prohibit for them only the foul; and he will relieve them of their burden and the fetters that they used to wear. Then those who believe in him, and honour him, and help him, and follow the light which is sent down with him: they are the successful

23:51.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلرُّسُلُ كُلُواْ مِنَ ٱلطَّيِّبَٰتِ وَٱعۡمَلُواْ صَٰلِحًاۖ إِنِّي بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ عَلِيمࣱ‏
23:51.en: O ye messengers! Eat of the good things, and do right. Lo! I am Aware of what ye do

eAUC-yvp1hk.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 8: Quranic Themes, Avoiding Fawahish
eAUC-yvp1hk.one_line: Why Muslims must refuse the normalization of fawahish, drawn from Al-A'raf: the five categories of haram, Lut's people and wife, and the Prophet who lifts burdens.
eAUC-yvp1hk.summary: He argues that the sharpest moral difference between Muslims and modern society is over sexual expression outside marriage. Norms were shifted over decades by changing what society accepts, and constant exposure through films and media slowly moves Muslims from tolerating others' choices to normalizing them for themselves, the way repeated exposure desensitizes the body. Islam does not hide sexuality: it is celebrated within marriage, while any expression outside it is fahisha, a specific category of sin distinct from sin in general. From 7:33 he lays out the five exclusive categories Allah forbade, stressing that public indecency is worse because it normalizes. From the story of Lut he shows a people who made purity itself shameful, and Lut's wife, who did not commit the act but was content with it and so perished. He separates treating people with dignity, as he does as a doctor, from approving their behaviour. From 7:157 he describes the Prophet as one who promotes good norms, permits the wholesome, forbids the filthy and removes burdens, so prohibitions are a mercy. He asks the community to hold a clear stance, educate its youth, and avoid everything near fahisha, including pornography and obscene speech.

outline.heading: Tonight's theme: avoiding fawahish
outline.gist: What once seemed a Western problem has now spread to every society, and this is where Muslims and the wider culture differ most.

outline.heading: How the moral line moved in the West
outline.gist: America began with Judeo-Christian sexual ethics, and over a century those who identified as liberals pushed the line until those values lost.

outline.heading: Change the norm and you change society
outline.gist: Persistence over time shifts what is acceptable, and the same method can shift it back, though it takes twice the effort.

outline.heading: The Quran refuses normalization
outline.gist: A central Quranic theme is naming fahisha as filth and refusing those who normalize it, a stance every Muslim must take.

outline.heading: Agreeing on much, differing sharply here
outline.gist: Western society got many things right by Islamic standards, but on this topic the difference could not be greater and must be stated clearly.

outline.heading: From adapting to normalizing
outline.gist: Muslims have adapted to relationships outside marriage in films and daily life, and adapting slowly becomes normalizing it for yourself.

outline.heading: Desensitization works on the mind
outline.gist: Just as daily images of murder numb people and the body can be desensitized to a stimulus, constant exposure numbs the conscience to fahisha.

outline.heading: Zina will never be acceptable
outline.gist: Tolerating others' choices is fine, but any sexual expression outside marriage between a man and a woman is never acceptable to Muslims.

outline.heading: Why open sexual expression harms
outline.gist: Sexuality is delicate and confusing from puberty to death, and trashing family values has visibly harmed homes and child-raising.

outline.heading: Sexuality celebrated within marriage
outline.gist: Islam does not ask you to be ashamed of it; weddings are celebrated with singing, and Allah gives intimacy its proper place.

outline.heading: What fahisha means
outline.gist: Ithm is the umbrella for all sin, while fahisha names a specific category of sexually oriented sin.

outline.heading: The community must educate itself
outline.gist: Muslims must learn how to handle this in schools, workplaces, politics and with children, and they are far behind.

outline.heading: Youth under pressure
outline.gist: High school students are questioned about their worth for not having partners, and mental health workers describe a growing epidemic.

outline.heading: Inventing claims in Allah's name
outline.gist: Allah forbade five exclusive categories; the last is speaking about Him without knowledge, the root of innovation, cults and religion for profit, alongside associating partners with Him.

outline.heading: Open and hidden indecency, sin and transgression
outline.gist: Public fahisha is worst because it normalizes the act for the community; hidden fahisha is still haram, as are sin in general and taking what is not yours.

outline.heading: Categories, not single acts
outline.gist: Each of the five is a category holding many forbidden behaviours, not one act.

outline.heading: Islam is taken as a whole
outline.gist: Even in Ramadan we speak about this, because the deen is accepted in full, the easy parts and the hard ones.

outline.heading: Sinners welcome, celebrating sin is not
outline.gist: The texts leave no room for interpretation; someone who commits fahisha is welcome in the masjid, but not to parade it.

outline.heading: Knowing where we differ makes coexistence possible
outline.gist: Neighbourly living depends on being clear about what we share and what we do not, and our boundaries are no longer respected.

outline.heading: Societies that loosened sexual norms declined
outline.gist: Rome, Persia and Indian kingdoms fell soon after sexual behaviour was opened without limits, which is why 7:33 states the prohibition exclusively.

outline.heading: A fahisha no one had normalized before
outline.gist: Lut's people were the first to publicly endorse the act and demand acceptance; he calls them musrifun, people who go too far.

outline.heading: Purity made shameful
outline.gist: They wanted Lut expelled for seeking purity, showing how minds can be pushed until cleanliness itself is frowned upon.

outline.heading: Lut's wife and the homes of prophets
outline.gist: Her fate is meant to unsettle; no prophet's household commits fahisha, so she did not do the act herself.

outline.heading: She perished for being content with it
outline.gist: She normalized what they did and stayed behind, while his daughters left because they kept saying it was wrong.

outline.heading: A physician's stance
outline.gist: In his clinic he treats every patient with dignity without preaching, yet outside it he holds the act to be haram and has the right to say so.

outline.heading: Respect people, refuse the behaviour
outline.gist: Like recreational drinking, we do not mistreat those who do it, but we never call it acceptable; that is the lesson of Lut's wife.

outline.heading: Musa's dua for good in both worlds
outline.gist: Musa asks Allah to write good for them in this life and the next, saying they have turned back to Him.

outline.heading: Turning back and the mercy that encompasses all
outline.gist: Hudna means turning back to Allah in guidance, the origin of their name; Allah replies that His mercy encompasses everything and is written for those with taqwa who give zakah and believe.

outline.heading: The unlettered Prophet foretold in Torah and Injil
outline.gist: Those worthy of that mercy follow the Prophet who could not read or write yet taught humanity, and whose description is in earlier scriptures.

outline.heading: Interlude
He promotes good norms and forbids harmful ones
outline.gist: Not every societal norm is positive; the Prophet encourages the good norms of a society and discourages the bad ones.

outline.heading: Wholesome things made lawful
outline.gist: Muslims can work with society on shared norms like reducing alcohol and smoking; the Prophet permits what is good in origin and beneficial.

outline.heading: Filthy things made unlawful
outline.gist: Eating is not discouraged, only excess; what he forbids are khaba'ith, acts from which no good comes.

outline.heading: Removing burdens and shackles
outline.gist: The fifth function lifts restrictions that earlier communities carried, for all time.

outline.heading: Prohibition as mercy
outline.gist: The deen does not aim to make life hard; a merciful Lord warns us of what ruins mind, heart, body and society so we can stand tall and reach our potential.

outline.heading: Do not even come near it
outline.gist: Many linguists define fahisha as the opposite of haya, a sensitivity to others' boundaries and to what causes shame.

outline.heading: The Prophet never spoke obscenely
outline.gist: Even when angry he never used foul words, because avoiding fahisha covers speech, sight and listening.

outline.heading: Pornography fuels exploitation
outline.gist: Consuming it supports an industry that abuses vulnerable young women; we are an ummah that avoids and refuses fahisha.

outline.heading: Outro

9:40.ar: إِلَّا تَنصُرُوهُ فَقَدۡ نَصَرَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِذۡ أَخۡرَجَهُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ ثَانِيَ ٱثۡنَيۡنِ إِذۡ هُمَا فِي ٱلۡغَارِ إِذۡ يَقُولُ لِصَٰحِبِهِۦ لَا تَحۡزَنۡ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مَعَنَاۖ فَأَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ سَكِينَتَهُۥ عَلَيۡهِ وَأَيَّدَهُۥ بِجُنُودࣲ لَّمۡ تَرَوۡهَا وَجَعَلَ كَلِمَةَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ ٱلسُّفۡلَىٰۗ وَكَلِمَةُ ٱللَّهِ هِيَ ٱلۡعُلۡيَاۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ
9:40.en: If ye help him not, still Allah helped him when those who disbelieve drove him forth, the second of two; when they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us. Then Allah caused His peace of reassurance to descend upon him and supported him with hosts ye cannot see, and made the word of those who disbelieved the nethermost, while Allah's Word it was that became the uppermost. Allah is Mighty, Wise

9:90.ar: وَجَآءَ ٱلۡمُعَذِّرُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡأَعۡرَابِ لِيُؤۡذَنَ لَهُمۡ وَقَعَدَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَبُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥۚ سَيُصِيبُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ مِنۡهُمۡ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمࣱ‏
9:90.en: And those among the wandering Arabs who had an excuse came in order that permission might be granted them. And those who lied to Allah and His messenger sat at home. A painful doom will fall on those of them who disbelieve

9:91.ar: لَّيۡسَ عَلَى ٱلضُّعَفَآءِ وَلَا عَلَى ٱلۡمَرۡضَىٰ وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَجِدُونَ مَا يُنفِقُونَ حَرَجٌ إِذَا نَصَحُواْ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦۚ مَا عَلَى ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلࣲۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
9:91.en: Not unto the weak nor unto the sick nor unto those who can find naught to spend is any fault (to be imputed though they stay at home) if they are true to Allah and His messenger. Not unto the good is there any road (of blame). Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

9:92.ar: وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا مَآ أَتَوۡكَ لِتَحۡمِلَهُمۡ قُلۡتَ لَآ أَجِدُ مَآ أَحۡمِلُكُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ تَوَلَّواْ وَّأَعۡيُنُهُمۡ تَفِيضُ مِنَ ٱلدَّمۡعِ حَزَنًا أَلَّا يَجِدُواْ مَا يُنفِقُونَ
9:92.en: Nor unto those whom, when they came to thee (asking) that thou shouldst mount them, thou didst tell: I cannot find whereon to mount you. They turned back with eyes flowing with tears, for sorrow that they could not find the means to spend

9:93.ar: ۞إِنَّمَا ٱلسَّبِيلُ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡتَـٔۡذِنُونَكَ وَهُمۡ أَغۡنِيَآءُۚ رَضُواْ بِأَن يَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلۡخَوَالِفِ وَطَبَعَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ فَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ

dKy-jGS7CFo.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 10: Quranic Themes, Courage
dKy-jGS7CFo.one_line: Courage in At-Tawbah: the Prophet in the cave, the tearful companions left behind at Tabuk, and the command that enemies find strength, not fear, in Muslims.
dKy-jGS7CFo.summary: He defines courage as moving forward despite fear and a real chance of harm, trusting that Allah sees and will not neglect you; only someone afraid can be brave, and courage is not rudeness. He hopes a generation raised outside tyranny will speak the truth. Through 9:40 he corrects a common reading of the cave: the Prophet told Abu Bakr not to be sad, not not to fear. He had planned every detail, yet the pursuers reached the very cave, and both expected to die. Abu Bakr's grief was for the mission and for the Prophet; the reply meant they had done all they could, so Allah was pleased with them, and they would meet their end with dignity. Allah then sent calm and turned the pursuers' eyes. From Tabuk (9:90-93) he contrasts the Bedouin excuse-makers with the poor who wept because they could not go, and the man who gave his honour in charity by forgiving everyone who had wronged him. Islam asks for calculated risk, not recklessness. Finally, from 9:123, Muslims should never be ashamed of the verses on combat; the ummah has been too predictable in its fear, though the last fifteen months showed a braver generation.

outline.heading: Opening
What courage means
outline.gist: Courage is going forward even when you expect harm, because you trust Allah sees, will reward you and will not neglect you; no one is proud of cowardice.

outline.heading: Only the afraid can be brave
outline.gist: Superman was never brave without kryptonite, Batman was; courage needs fear, and it also needs etiquette rather than rudeness.

outline.heading: A generation raised in fear
outline.gist: Growing up under a regime where free speech could cost your life, as in Sednaya, drains a people's courage; he hopes this generation will stand its ground.

outline.heading: The Quran brews courage
outline.gist: Tawakkul means doing everything you can, taking a calculated risk and leaving the rest to Allah.

outline.heading: A rebuke to those who stayed back from Tabuk
outline.gist: The verse came almost a decade after the Hijrah, addressing those in Madinah who would not face the far stronger Romans.

outline.heading: Allah supported him before
outline.gist: If you will not stand by him, Allah already did, when he was driven out as the second of two.

outline.heading: La tahzan means do not be sad
outline.gist: Huzn is never fear in Arabic, and the Quran pairs the two as distinct, so the Prophet told Abu Bakr not to grieve, not not to be afraid.

outline.heading: He did everything to avoid capture
outline.gist: The relaxed-hero version of the story removes the lesson; he left at midday, masked, went the opposite way, covered tracks and hid three nights in an ordinary cave.

outline.heading: They found the cave
outline.gist: Against all odds the pursuers climbed the right mountain and entered the very cave while the two crouched in a tiny inner hollow.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's grief
outline.gist: He was afraid, but his sorrow was that the plan had failed and the hoped-for state in Madinah would end in a cave, and that he could not protect the Prophet.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr circling to guard him
outline.gist: On the road he kept moving behind, beside and ahead of the Prophet, saying he was only one man while the Prophet was the hope of the world.

outline.heading: Allah is with us: we did our best
outline.gist: The words meant Allah was pleased with their choices; all He asks is your best, and if it fails you have still succeeded, so they would face death with dignity.

outline.heading: Calm and unseen soldiers
outline.gist: Allah sent His tranquillity and unseen help; narrations mention a web and a dove, and a man relieved himself beside a hole that would have revealed them.

outline.heading: Allah turned their eyes away
outline.gist: He controls every glance; he imagines the pursuers learning later that their target had been right beneath them.

outline.heading: He was never promised he would survive
outline.gist: The Prophet believed he was about to die as a martyr and still showed courage; Allah made the word of the disbelievers lowest.

outline.heading: Hijrah as the ummah's rebirth
outline.gist: Umar began the calendar with the Hijrah rather than the birth or the prophethood because that day both the Prophet and the ummah were reborn.

outline.heading: Tabuk, the army of hardship
outline.gist: Facing a Roman army of over 25,000, the Prophet called everyone who could afford a mount to march a thousand kilometres in August heat before the harvest.

outline.heading: Giving whatever they had
outline.gist: He spread his cloak for donations; some brought a handful of dates or a little food, the last thing in their homes.

outline.heading: The excuse-makers who stayed back
outline.gist: Some Bedouins lied about wealth and illness to be excused; qa'ada here means staying back from the stand one should have taken.

outline.heading: No blame on the weak, sick and poor
outline.gist: Those who cannot go or give carry no blame so long as they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger.

outline.heading: The man who gave his honour in charity
outline.gist: With nothing to give, a companion forgave everyone who had harmed or insulted him so the army could march spiritually lighter.

outline.heading: His charity accepted
outline.gist: Next morning the Prophet asked three times for the man who gave his honour, then told him Allah had accepted it as charity.

outline.heading: Those who left in tears
outline.gist: Men begged for mounts and weapons, and when the Prophet had nothing left they walked away with tears running down their faces.

outline.heading: The blame falls on the wealthy who stayed
outline.gist: Those with means who asked to be excused had their hearts sealed; it took bravery to set out against the Romans, and bravery to weep at being left behind.

outline.heading: Rewarded though held back
outline.gist: The Prophet said people in Madinah shared every step of the march because only a valid excuse kept them home.

outline.heading: Calculated risk, not recklessness
outline.gist: Those without provision were not allowed to walk along, since that endangers others; reward is for courage, not for running into fire.

outline.heading: Never be ashamed of the verses on combat
outline.gist: Nothing in the Quran calls for open-ended violence or forced conversion; extremist readings exist in every ideology, and these are verses of bravery.

outline.heading: Let them find strength in you
outline.gist: Enemies must see grit, not fear; the ummah has become predictable, quieted by a bill or a political threat.

outline.heading: A generation that was not afraid
outline.gist: In the last fifteen months students camped at universities and accepted the cost, shifting the needle; that strength must continue.

V80gcyutDhk.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 3: Reflection and Contemplation
V80gcyutDhk.one_line: Contemplation as a forgotten act of worship: its Quranic basis, the Prophet's retreats in Hira and i'tikaf, and practical methods to do it.
V80gcyutDhk.summary: Taking the fourth rule of tazkiyah, he explains that he once assumed everyone reflects, then found most people never do. The Quran repeatedly calls for tafakkur and tadabbur, and early Muslims ranked an hour of contemplation above a night of prayer and called it a mirror showing one's good and bad. His central example is the Prophet walking hours to the cave of Hira for months, overlooking the sky and the Kaaba and wrestling with existential questions until revelation came. We inherit the answers, yet the Prophet kept contemplating through i'tikaf all year round, which he contrasts with treating i'tikaf as a sleepover. He laments that Muslims look to yogis and stoics for something that is their own, and blames phones for killing the daydreaming that once forced people to think. Contemplation untangles a ball of yarn or catches loose birds one at a time; recurring thoughts are unfinished business. Practically, choose a quiet time, slow the heart rate, isolate one thought, then either walk around it from different angles, journalling the answers, or run scenarios to see which response leads to a good outcome. He insists ideas are not pills: without dedicated reflection nothing taught will change anyone.

outline.heading: Recap of the rules of tazkiyah
outline.gist: Apply everything to yourself, try the exercises, keep a growing daily portion, and reflect, which is today's topic.

outline.heading: Reflection in the Quran
outline.gist: He found most people do not reflect at all; the Quran calls for standing for Allah then thinking, for contemplating creation, and for pondering its verses, using several terms.

outline.heading: An hour of contemplation outweighs a night of prayer
outline.gist: Early Muslims said this, something they could only have learned from the Prophet's teaching.

outline.heading: Contemplation is a mirror
outline.gist: It shows a person their good and bad, and one who reflects learns from everything they witness.

outline.heading: The arrogant are turned away from reflecting on the signs
outline.gist: An early scholar read the verse as being distracted from contemplation; long reflection leads to Paradise, and two thoughtful rakaat beat a night of absent-hearted prayer.

outline.heading: The Prophet's walk to the cave of Hira
outline.gist: He chose a distant, high cave hours from home with an open view of the sky, the land and the Kaaba.

outline.heading: What he did in the cave for months
outline.gist: At forty, dissatisfied with how people lived and full of existential questions, he stayed for weeks with nothing but his thoughts, with Khadijah bringing food.

outline.heading: Revelation came in the place of reflection
outline.gist: Jibril came while he contemplated; we inherit his answers about purpose, yet he never stopped contemplating.

outline.heading: I'tikaf as the Prophet's year-round practice
outline.gist: I'tikaf was designed for contemplation and was not only for Ramadan; he screened off a space in the masjid by his door.

outline.heading: I'tikaf is devotion, not a sleepover
outline.gist: Bringing pillows and phones to the masjid is not i'tikaf; it means total devotion to one thing, with long hours of thought beyond prayer and recitation.

outline.heading: Contemplation is ours, not imported
outline.gist: It hurts him that Muslims seek it from yogis or stoics when the Prophet received prophethood through it.

outline.heading: How phones killed daydreaming
outline.gist: Before phones, boredom forced people to stare out the window and let the mind and heart process together.

outline.heading: We reflect at the wrong times
outline.gist: People do it under stress while driving or at the family table; a Muslim needs dedicated time, and it is a skill most never learned.

outline.heading: Untangling the ball of yarn
outline.gist: Seek clarity by gently pulling one thread at a time; a recurring thought is the mind's unfinished business demanding closure first.

outline.heading: Catching the birds one at a time
outline.gist: Thoughts fly around until caught and caged one by one; chasing them all catches none.

outline.heading: Values and a sound heart come only through reflection
outline.gist: Values and a stable, joyful subconscious are produced by no other means.

outline.heading: Setting the scene: time, calm, one thought
outline.gist: Pick a quiet time, slow your heart rate with breathing, set other thoughts aside, and start with any nagging thought.

outline.heading: Method one: looking from every angle
outline.gist: Abstract concepts like humility need a 3D form in the mind; ask where it comes from, why it is needed, how it helps or harms and how to practise it.

outline.heading: Journal your answers: the notebooks from Syria
outline.gist: Leaving Syria with two suitcases, one was full of his notebooks; write down what you reach, even in a phone's notes.

outline.heading: Method two: running scenarios
outline.gist: Play out responses like a short film until one leads to an outcome you like; aggression and domination always end badly.

outline.heading: Make peace with the mind's chaos
outline.gist: The brain works randomly; contemplation puts a train on the tracks so answers arrive later, even while driving.

outline.heading: Answers can take months
outline.gist: The Prophet spent months in Hira and kept taking days off for i'tikaf to think through problems.

outline.heading: Ideas are not pills
outline.gist: Scholars have said the same things for a thousand years; people do not change because they take ideas at face value without reflecting.
